A fun and interesting concept, perhaps under-realized.

Orwell is less of a game and more of a scenario; you are given the role of an NSA data analyst (by another name) who, in the aftermath of a terrorist incident, is given the investigative assignment and jurisdiction to peer into the lives of several suspects with various ties to the event and each other - with a set of invasive and controversial tools.

What I liked:
- The ambience. The music was, for the most part, ethereal and relaxing, and the graphics minimalistic yet evocative. 
- The theme, overall. If you can suspend your disbelief you can effectively see how this scenario would play out in real life, and it exposes you to the very necessary dialogue about personal freedom in this day and age, though I have some issue with how it’s expressed (see below).

What I thought could be better:
- Linearity. The game itself is mostly a tunnel. That’s fine if it’s the developer’s desire to tell a story, but investigations in real life are rarely so straightforward - it was a frustrating inconsistency for me.
- Datachunks, and their purpose. Datachunks are the game’s terminology for data points that you gather from various places; this is *the* gameplay here and I have to admit I was a bit underwhelmed. They aren’t explained very well to begin with. The role of conflicting datachunks isn’t well understood even as you’re finishing the game and there seems to be little to no penalty for assimilating bad information. Add to that the fact that the chunks themselves are pretty limited and spelled out for you (in blue and yellow highlighting against the page), and it makes for a pretty pedestrian mechanic. I was still able to suspend my disbelief enough to finish the story, but I couldn’t help think that a little more complexity and freedom and a little more trust in the player would reap a more satisfying conclusion.
- The story itself has zero sympathetic characters and several predictable plot points. The overall theme of ‘limitless government overreach’ comes at you with all the nuance of a sledgehammer. I guess that’s to be expected when the name of the game is literally ‘Orwell,’ and sometimes sledgehammers can even be fun; but if you’re looking for a multifaceted and deep exploration of this topic in a game format, I think we’re still waiting.

The point: 6.5/10.
Is it the most complete and satisfying gameplay possible? Probably not. But like most story-centric indie titles I think the concept is what is most important; it is fertile subject matter and I’d love to see it further explored, perhaps even in an episodic format. It took me about 4.5 hours to finish and apparently that is dead average, so use that for your own personal evaluation of whether the price you pay is worth it. Recommended, with qualifications.

[i]Orwell[/i] is a text-based game that puts you in the shoes of a crowdsourced cybersurveillance data clerk.

So, in the late 2000s The Nation has been suffering from a spiralling crime rate and unstable neighbours. This propelled the notoriously authoritarian Party to power, who then passed the vague-named Safety Bill. Basically, The Nation is an Americanish country that is careening towards a police state: the Safety Bill allows the government unlimited remote access to any electronic device they can identify, and extended detentions without charge for even slightly unfortunate turns of phrase. They have bots that can sift through that data for those unfortunate phrases. However, knowing the kind of jinn they are letting out the bottle, they created the solution: ORWELL, and you. As the anonymous Investigator, a foreign citizen, you are to evaluate the “datachunks” the automated system highlights among the information on designated target persons. The police only see the datachunks you feed into the system, and will generally take them literally; they can send you texts, but that’s it. It’s up to you to balance nuance, ethics and expedience, and to choose what to submit and what not to submit.

This gives you quite a bit of liberty. You can be the zealous [i]chekist[/i], using your omnipotent tools to not crush bones but crush souls, helping the police ravage through people’s lives. You can be the manipulator, minimizing the collateral damage and keeping the often trigger-happy police from harming their own cause. Or you can go full rebel and do your best to sabotage the investigation.

Now, as a bombing kills several people, and an apparently radicalized anti-surveillance group seems to be behind it in a massive bout of irony, you are to put your Internet detective hat on, and validate the system in a trial by fire, and a race against the clock.

Beyond the sometimes counterintuitive plot twists, I’ve found no issues with the game.

You’ll probably like it if you liked [i]Papers, Please[/i].

The game interface is very cool, though. It's sleek and really fun to navigate. This is a game where your choices definitely matter. So do good deductive reasoning skills. I will update this at some point after I've played it again, because I will definitely play it again. There's just so much information. It's very in-depth and thorough. 

Once you've finished the game, you have access to all five chapters of your already played game. This is pretty cool if you just want to be able to go back and see the alternate endings.

[h1]A memorable and engaging experience.[/h1]

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator working for a police state. The goal is to identify and build a case against suspected terrorists using both publicly available and personal/confidential information. Information you upload enables access to further sources. Uploading mention of a notable injury will unlock access to the person's medical records; finding a phone number or email lets you spy in on their correspondence etc. 

But information you upload could be incorrect, or misinterpreted/twisted to suit the government's agenda. How far will you go? Who will you condemn?

[h1]How is it?[/h1]

This core is compelling and unique enough to carry the game through to its conclusion. The comparisons to Papers Please are obvious, but Orwell is far more expansive. Where Papers Please created tension by pitting you against a time limit, Orwell creates a complex, intriguing and politically relevant narrative where you never truly know who is or isn't guilty. It is hard to discuss in detail without spoiling, but the story is full of twists and turns and finds a way to successfully play out dramatic scenes that you experience from behind the safety of your computer screen and the shield of Orwell.

The soundtrack compliments the game nicely, and is used effectively to punctuate important revelations in the story.

It's entirely text-based, and game length depends entirely on your reading speed and habits. Speed-reading and scanning for pertinent information (which the game highlights for you) can shorten the game to 3-4 hours. A more thorough and careful reading, especially if read aloud, can extend your playtime to 8 hours. The game will be a one-time experience for most players, but the game lets you play each episode individually once cleared, and there's enough agency in what optional & conflicting information you upload that replayability is there for those that want it.

[h1]However[/h1]

The game has enough flaws to feel like it wasn't thoroughly tested.

Conflicting information is highlighted in yellow, rather than blue. You can only upload one of these, so the game highlights conflicting information before you've identified what it conflicts with. This is both a minor spoiler and very awkward, and could have easily been handled better.

It's easy to get overwhelmed with information. The game highlights sources with new information for you, but distinguishing between what is optional and mandatory to upload is not obvious. Perhaps this is intentional, but it is too easy to be stuck in a deadlock with 30 possible sources to go through trying to find the one piece of mandatory information you refrained from uploading the first time. An additional icon highlighting old sources with uploadable information would have made this much less tedious.

Spying in on peoples phone conversations happens in real time. This has a wonderful voyeuristic feel to it, but the conversations progress far too fast to read aloud at a comfortable speaking pace. This would be fine if they didn't contain time-sensitive information that needs to be uploaded during the conversation itself. Anyone streaming this or reading aloud to themselves will be caught in the awkward spot of either missing the window to upload information, or have to voice act far too fast for the conversation to sound natural.

Finally, the writing itself is simply poor. I wonder if it was written by a native English speaker or a trained writer. The grammar is awkward, misleading or just incorrect far too often, and this does detract from the otherwise believable world and engaging story the game creates. Simple proof-reading would have solved this.

None of these are game-breaking or significantly ruin the game, but all are so needless, so simply and easily solved that their inclusions are frustrating.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

If you liked Papers Please, find the theme compelling or want a unique text-based game, you'll enjoy this. It comes with too many niggling issues to recommend at full price, but with a small discount this will be a worthwhile experience that will stay with you for years to come.

It's the first time I give a revew on Steam but I feel I had to do it for this game. I bought it this week and started playing yesterday. I stopped at 3 am to go to bed, then continued playing today as I was completely hooked. I did a complete playthrough in 9.5 hours, which is really great for the price. It could take less time, but I really got invested in the story and actually took time to make every decision carefully. 

TL;DR : This game is a masterpiece. Buy it.
I'll try to break down my impressions :

PROS
-AMAZING storyline! It was intricate, well written, complex... I enjoy puzzles & solving enigmas, I'm not new to it... but this game got me wandering in the dark, completely distabilized. And the side stories just adds to it.
-Well written characters! The game is litterally about digging into targetted people's life, going as deep as possible. It could have been so bad, it could have been superficial data made up just for the story. But it was interesting. You have to make choices, decide what information you give up to Orwell and what other info you keep to yourself, and it impacts the story and these people's life. I developped sympathy for some and aversion for others. The characters felt real.
-The ending was great. At that point, I was expecting it, but it was still so satisfying.
-Very intuitive and easy gameplay. Just a tip : don't go too fast. Wait a bit before sending a piece of information, try to make up your own opinion with other infos first.
-Nice art style. It's simple yet beautiful, I really enjoyed it. 
-Nice soundtrack. The music was always appropriate and guided me through the story. 

CONS
-Only one story. I wish there was more enigmas, I wish it wasn't over! Even if I could change the playthrough slightly, it's still the same. I'm eager to play more of this game!
-Some bugs. Was never really detrimental to my gaming experience, but still slightly annoying. I sometimes had trouble dragging the infos to the dropping box, and somtimes there was the alert symbol like I sill had unseen data chunks, which wasn't true, so I would search for missed info that weren't there. 

CONCLUSION
If you're the kind of player to aggressively click your mouse at every dialogue box to skip it as fast as possible, this game is not for you. It's a game for the critical thinkers, for people who like to pause to think and come up with theories. You have to enjoy reading, because that's basically all what you'll do... it's more of a graphic novel than a video game. But it's so delicously done, if you're open to something different and refreshing, don't hesitate any further, buy this game and dive into it. You won't regret it I promise. :)

You play through this game incredibly fast, but as someone who's a massive fan of everything dystopian, this is an absolutely brilliant concept! You get to decide on what will happen to people based on your own first impressions and what the media writes about them. You have to judge based on intuition and you'll notice at one point or another that you might judge too quickly because certain people might be in your allergy-space or because they might've written a regrettable facebook message. 
I really really hope that the developers will put out more stories with this concept (even though there is a bit of a closed ending) because I absolutely loved the gameplay of it and the decision making involved with it.

This is my personal opinion on the game and I am going to talk about a few reasons that I would recommend this game.

A few things that make this game great:
[*] A quasi-realistic and relatable world for most people, the artstyle is pleasing. I personally find the "transparent" feel as representing how Orwell oversees everything. Characters might start off as stereotypical but are psychogically developed during the course of the story.

[*] Your choices do affect the ending to a certain degree 

[*] The fact that you play as an outsider to the system is thought-provoking and you can oversee the outcomes of your choices and question the ethics and utility of your actions

[*] The plot-twists were attractive and made me more eager to keep on reading




Here are a few points that displeased me: 

[*] You might not like this if you are not ready to examine and read long text chunks, there are some information that seem boring some will not even bother to read (but still relevant to the world building in the game)

[*] Some choices leading to certain outcomes may not seem logical and unpredictable, making the gamer confused and maybe frustrated to a certain level. [spoiler]For instance, Nina being killed or not in the game due to signaling that she has a weapon didn't make much sense to me.[spoiler] 

[*]There is a time in the story that can feel stagnating and boring since you might have to review information already seen previously in order to get new ones. 


Conclusion: I would recommend this game for people who have some time to spend, and like investigative games who isn't afraid of going into details. Also, if you are a fan of dystopian stories and interested in problems related to surveillance.

When playing this game, understand that you are not merely playing a game, you are witnessing literature unfold in front of your eyes.

You will be exposed to the virtues and follies of a mass surveillance system. You will witness the good intentions behind this system, the potential for power abuse and how it affects the lives of not just the guilty and all who are related to him/her. You will witness how this system can be exploited, how even it is not perfect. 

And finally, at the end, after you have witnessed the good and ills of the mass surveillance system as you participate in its usage, you will be presented with a question: is the use of mass surveillance system truly justifiable? 

I am still pondering about this question.
It's a bit more linear than I thought it would be, for a game with data mining elements I was hoping for a more open world experience. Despite it's a Great Value game for the price.

Loosely based on '1984', the critically acclaimed dystopian novel by George Orwell about state surveillance and the horrors that unavoidably come with it, 'Orwell' delivers an immersing story taking five or six hours to complete. You are an investigater looking for information about recent terrorist activities, which will hopefully lead to the arrest of the perpetrators. But information does not necessarily equal facts...

If you are interested in topics like politics, freedom, security, and ethics, this game is well worth your time. Most choices you get to make don't matter that much, it's all in the narrative that is frighteningly close to what is happening right now in most countries in the world; hundreds of thousands of people worldwide evaluating and interpreting the actions of all people in the vicinity of camera's, phone's or computers. This game shows how easy it can be to find these people guilty of something. Anyone.

Nice artwork, great writing and plot twists. Nicely disconcerting music. Interface is sometimes a little clogged (lots of scrolling), but clear and fluid.

Good reads on this topic are 'Little brother' by Cory Doctorow and Philip K Dick's 'Minority report'.

TL;DR the famous quote "Any society that would give up a little liberty to gain a little security, will deserve neither and lose both" by Benjamin Franklin is explained by this game. 9/10

Orwell is part-hacking, part-detective sim which satisfies both those unrealised career desires for me, but which does get repetitive. The concept is great. You're essentially an NSA agent for some generic authoritarian state, trying to prevent terrorist attacks. You scour documents, social media pages, snoop through emails and listen in on phone calls, putting all the pieces together to build a profile of the terrorist organisation. The moral choices come in when you can decide what information to provide to your colleagues and what, if any, to conceal. The UI is basic but feels smooth. The gameplay consists of reading through these sources until the game highlights information of importance for you, and you decide whether or not to put it on record. After the initial novelty wears off this can get tedious because it's too easy. I was longing for real detective work, but found myself mindlessly clicking through sources until the game showed me something, because the need for you to really think about where and what you're looking for most of the time just isn't there. Sound design is...OK. Suitable ambient background tones until you hit a breakthrough and send out the troops. Voice acting would have been a great addition to the wiretapping segments, because...

Despite all this I didn't get bored. Why? Because the characterisation in this game is spot on. I was amazed at how much I found myself invested in some of the people I was investigating. Characters formed only from pieces of text on a screen and an impressionistic picture. You get to read into these people's lives, into their social media personas, their private correspondence, and the depth here was delightful. I found myself laughing at the detail written into the Not-Facebook profiles and the musician's website. The game might not be fully realised; it has mechanics limitations and content gets explored fully early on, leaving it stale fairly quickly, but if you like playing detective there is definitely enough material to keep you amused for a few hours.

I just finshed playing Orwell for the first time and personally, I already want to dive back in, but maybe that's just me. If you are going to enjoy this game, it helps if you have read 1984 by George Orwell (all the quotes in the game are from the book and the subject of the game deals heavily with subject of state surviellance and control.)

Orwell is essentially a similator that allows you to use a version of the kind of Big Data surviellence tools that the NSA uses, such as PRISM. You can look at web pages, snoop on chats and phone calls and hack into phones and machines if you can get the IP.

The way the game is actually played is you sift through the various sources you have at your disposal and upload chunks of information to Orwell. Because the intelligence agency can only see the data that you point to as relevant, what data you upload will have a big effect on the outcome of the game.

Fortunately though, Orwell highlights the bits of intelligence (chunks) as you go through the page, which makes it a it easier.

Essentially then, Orwell is a game about being employed as an intelligence analyst. What data you feed to the government will determine who gets arrrested and who lives and dies if you don't get to the bomber.

Having only played through once, I am not sure how much replay value Orwell has. Given the large amount of text, I suspect that if you waited a few weeks and went back to it, you would find new things. I certainly did not get the optimal ending the first time.

Personally, I cannot reccomend this game highly enough. The platform that it is built on could be used to make so many other stories and scenarios, so I really hope they have Stem workshop access.

However, keep in mind that Orwell is a highly cerebral game that involves alot of reading. If you are not really into Intelligence as a subject, you might not get it.

On the other hand, if you are an Intel nerd, then you will love Orwell, which imho, is kind of like the new Uplink. 

Enjoy.

[h1]General[/h1]

This is [b]not really a game.[/b] Most of the time you would only be pointing out "data chunks" to relevant character, and the said data chunks has been conveniently pointed out to you by the highlight, so you can't miss it. The only time you get a little pressure is on the final episode, when there are "data upload" limit imposed on you.

[h1]There is minimal gameplay[/h1]
There is minimal gameplay, as it is mostly just drag and drop something. The clues are too easily pointed out to you. Sometimes there are some conflicting data, but it is easy to resolve this kind of things. It is also bad that you don't know how the data chunks you are given is processed. A wrong data chunk could suddenly net a very violent response although previous data chunks you have given it is not the way. 


[h1]Story-Rich Gameplay[/h1]
However, the story in the game is excellent. It is not overly long and complicated, but it is quite complicated enough to keep you guessing on who is who and what is the truth beneath all of these things. All of the characters are alive, and the way they are chatting with each other, with you snooping in, at times make you guilty for snooping on someone's conversation. You will also see another person's life, and at times you will feel guilty that you are the one that send them into prison, sometimes by bending the truth so they can be arrested. And seeing their hobbies and their life, but watching their conversation, their blogs, or their social medias, sometimes makes you really hopeful that this guy/girl is not guilty so you could release them, and make you guilty if you have to arrest them.

[h1]Politics and Mass Surveillance[/h1]
Of course, this game is quite a political game, on the issue of mass surveillance. It subtly asks the player on how far the government could go in the name of security, and how is privacy should be treated if you have connection with a terror group. The game beautifully does not refer to any country or any political party (though a subtle jab at "Freedom" and "Peacekeeping" is done). 

Overall a beautiful game.

I know this is a long review but bare with me. So. This game. If I had to describe it in one word, I'd use Amazing. I bought it today as it was on sale and what the hell, right? 1984 is one of my favorite books and this takes the concept and executes it uniquely. Highly recommend,

Pros:

  - Characters are loveable - I never feel attachments to characters in games or feel bad or good over their fate, this game proves there are exceptions to every rule.
  - Graphics are unique and provide a change to next gen games.
  - The interface, for the most part (will be addressed in cons as well), was beautiful and seemless.
  - Investigation can be difficullt and provides a challenge that I throughly enjoyed. 
  - Gives you the feeling that your choices matter; it makes you stew over your choice, trying to predict the outcome and determine its desirability. Spoiler alert: [spoiler] your choices do matter! Make them wisely! [/spoiler]

Cons:

Orwell is a relitivly short point and click game based around you being a govenment agent that spys on the populace. Over the course of the game you will attempt to discover who is responsible for a recent bomb attack at a public location.

As the game progresses over the course of it's five chapters you will see your actions affect the outcome of the story and how characters act to one another. However, the story isn't very deep, nor are the characters always very fleashed out. The real focus of the game is it's tone, which it drives hope esspecially well twords the end of the game.

If you are a fan of Papers Please's tone and gameplay I would highly recomend this to you.

The game took me about five hours to complete, one per chapter. 

At the price at the time of writing ($10 USD) I would recomend purchasing it, even if you are only a little bit interested.

Orwell is a game where you played as an Investigator who look into series of terror attack against 'the nation'. You will be helped by the new surveillance system 'Orwell', a programm that can hack and wiretape electronic devices in the entire country. Your job is to sort the information that Orwell gives you and send it to an Advisor who will report your findings to the authority. For 5 days you will search through emails, phone call, and internet post of people who may be connected with the terror attack. Informations you send to the advidor may or may not be affect the course of the story.

Personally I find the story very interesting. The story delve into the classical dilemma of security vs privacy and every decision you make will determine the fate of people you investigate. That's pretty much what I can say about the story since I don't want to spoil anything. Gamplaywise it's pretty much a visual novel since what you doing most of the time is reading informations Orwell provided for you. So if you dislike reading, try the demo first before you decide.

If I have to criticize the game I will say it lacks of fail option. I wish there was an option where you give false informations and fail the game completely or get 'fired' (disappeared w/o trace).
Absolutely amazing interactive experience, would recommend it to everyone but dont watch youtube videos on it as it will be ruined for you , 10/10 game
